newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain could go for months without new Cuba envoy.
newsitem.headline: Spain could go for months without new Cuba envoy.

text.p: Spain, anxious to defuse a high-profile row over demands for democratic reforms in Cuba, said on Monday it might be months before it attempts to replace its outgoing ambassador to Havana.
Cuba, angered by Madrid's insistent hard line against its communist government, last week withdrew the so-called "placet" or approval it had given in October for new envoy Jose Coderch.
A Spanish foreign ministry official said on Monday a replacement would be appointed only once Cuba indicates willingness to accept the candidate.

"We have to look for a new ambassador. But we have to be sure if we present one, it will be acceptable. That will take a few months, I'm sure," the official told Reuters. "Spain is not in a rush to present a new one if the former one was rejected."
Havana accused Spain last week of "flagrant interference" in its affairs and said Coderch would not be welcome after all.

The crisis erupted after weeks of pressure by the new conservative government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar for a toughening of European Union policy towards Fidel Castro's one-party communist government.
Cuba was also angered by an interview Coderch had given to Spanish newspaper ABC in which he said the doors of the Spanish embassy in Havana would be open to visits by dissidents.
The foreign ministry official said there was no indication of a softening in Cuba's attitude regarding its ambassador.

In another sign that Spain has no interest in escalating tension, diplomatic sources in Madrid said they thought the government was unlikely to retaliate for the slight as long as Cuba takes no further action.
The outgoing Spanish ambassador, Edualdo Mirapeix, is due to fly out of Cuba in a few days' time, leaving the embassy's charge d'affaires as the top diplomat until a new envoy is appointed.
The foreign ministry official in Madrid said the government would not change its Cuba policy and would continue pressing for democratic reforms and increased pluralism.
"There is no change in policy. We are not going to change or tone down what we were saying before," he said.
A Western diplomat in Madrid said Spain appeared to be interested in the substance of policy rather than in escalating the fight.
Spain's non-confrontational approach did not constitute backing down because Madrid had not changed its policy, he said.
Spain welcomed Monday's formal approval by EU ministers of its suggestion to adopt a harder line toward Cuba.

The official policy paper, rubberstamped by finance ministers meeting in Brussels, said the bloc would actively seek opportunities to remind Cuban authorities both publicly and privately of basic responsibilities on human rights, in particular freedom of speech and association.
It also pledged to intensify talks with Cuban authorities and other sectors of society "to promote respect for human rights and real progress towards pluralist democracy."
